50--- In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools developed
51--- in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a small
52--- programming language, Imp.
53-
54--- - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with an
55---   *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that specifies the
56---   *operational semantics* of programs.
57-
58---   The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key features of
59---   full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the fundamental
60---   notion of mutable state and some common control structures.
61-
62--- - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the sense
63---   that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather than of
64---   particular programs in the language. These included:
65-
66---   - determinism of evaluation
67-
68---   - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions (e.g.,
69---     functional and relational definitions of arithmetic expression evaluation)
70-
71---   - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
72-
73---   - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of useful
74---     program transformations
75-
76---   - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
77-
78--- If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of tools
79--- for defining and discussing programming languages and language features
80--- that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work with, applied
81--- to a set of key properties. All of these properties are things that
82--- language designers, compiler writers, and users might care about knowing.
83--- Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our understanding of the
84--- programming languages we deal with that we might not consciously recognize
85--- them as "theorems." But properties that seem intuitively obvious can
86--- sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also subtly wrong!).
87-
88--- In another volume of this series (*Type Systems*), we expand upon the theme
89--- of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss *types* and
90--- *type soundness*. In this chapter, though, we turn to a different set of
91--- issues.
92-
93--- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
94--- simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
95--- definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
96--- particular specifications of their behavior.
97-
98--- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
99--- shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
100--- constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used
101--- to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs involving this
102--- construct.
103-
104--- Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject of
105--- intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core of a
106--- multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to specify
107--- and verify real software systems.
108-
109--- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
110--- *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
111--- proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications --
112--- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors
113--- the structure of the programs that they are about.
114-

123---

127---           - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
128---           - evaluation relation (for commands)
129---
130---      - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
131---          - determinism of evaluation
132---          - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
133---            definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
134---            arithmetic expression evaluation)
135---          - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
136---          - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
137---          - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
138---
139---      We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
140---        - Termination
141---        - Nontermination
142---        - Equivalence
143---

145---        - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
146---          correctness_ of programs in Imp
147---
148---      Goals:
149---        - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
150---        - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
151---

159--- ## Assertions
160-
161--- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory --
162--- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
163-
164-open scoped MyGetElem
165-
166-abbrev Assertion := State → Prop
167-
168--- Note to developers:
169---     HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the quiz/optional exercise
170---     so that there would be some modeling of the kinds of answers we expect.
171-
172--- For example,
173-
174--- - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value of `X` is `3`,
175--- - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
176--- - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
177-

197-def assertion2 : Assertion :=
198-  fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]

200-  fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧
201-            ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])

206--- 2. The value of X is 3 or is less or equal than the value of Y.
207--- 3. The value of Z is the integer square root of X.

212--- ### Notations for Assertions
213-
214--- This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two reasons:
215--- (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to begin with
216--- `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that we ever use to
217--- look up variables in assertions (we will almost never need to talk about
218--- two different memory states at the same time). For discussing examples
219--- informally, we'll adopt some simplifying conventions: we'll drop the
220--- initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus,
221--- instead of writing
222-
223---   fun st => st[X] = m
224-
225--- we'll write just
226-
227---   {{ X = m }}.
228-
229--- Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
230--- assertion. We'll see more examples below.
231-
232--- This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout the
233--- Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like `X`,
234--- `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`, `y`, `m`,
235--- and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is why, when
236--- translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with `st[X]` but leave
237--- `m` alone.

267--- The convention described above can be implemented with a little syntax
268--- magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
269--- `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts `Aexp`s,
270--- numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear between the
271--- `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an expression is
272--- `Assertion`.
273-

306---     There is now a custom entry [assn] for defining the syntax of

338-  match stx with
339-  | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
340-    let t ← elabTerm t none
341-    let ty ← Meta.inferType t
342-    -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
343-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
344-      return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
345-        (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
346-        (mkConst ``String)
347-        (mkConst ``Nat)
348-        (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
349-          (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
350-          (mkConst ``String)
351-          (mkConst ``Nat))
352-        (← elabTerm st none) t
353-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
354-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
355-    else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then  -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
356-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
357-    else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
358-      return t
359-    else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
360-      return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
361-    else
362-      return t
363-  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax

366-macro_rules
367-  | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))

369-macro_rules
370-  | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))
371-  | `(assn($st; $l = $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) = assn($st; $r))
372-  | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
373-  | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
374-  | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
375-  | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
376-  | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
377-  | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
378-  | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
379-  | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
380-  | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
381-  | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
382-  | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
383-  | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
384-  | `(assn($st; $f $args*)) => do
385-    let mut result := f
386-    for arg in args do
387-      result ← `($result assn($st; $arg))
388-    return result
389-end

415--- Function applications inside assertions automatically interpret their
416--- arguments in the current state. Thus, `{{ f e1 ... en }}` stands for
417--- `fun st => f (e1 st) ... (en st)`.
418-
419--- Occasionally it is simpler to write an assertion directly as a Lean
420--- function. Such a function can be placed inside the assertion notation
421--- without an escape marker.
422-
423--- For example, `{{ fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0 }}` indicates an assertion that
424--- every variable maps to `0` in the given state.
425-
426--- Note to developers:
427---     NOTATION: SAZ 2024: It is important that this custom notation be at a
428---     level higher than 1 when added to the `constr` grammar because it
429---     interacts with the "application" case of `com` and the notation for
430---     Hoare triples. That grammar parses embedded function arguments at level
431---     1. We never want `f {{P}}` to parse `{ P }` as an assertion when used
432---     in a command. Instead we want `{{P}}` to "close" the Hoare triple.
433---
434---     `NOTATION: Note for Rocq custom grammar hackers.  From what I can tell, the
435---     Rocq LL(1) parser does left-factorize the grammar, *however* it uses a very
436---     strict notion of what counts as "equal" for the purposes of the factorization.
437---     In particular, a grammar entry might have a level,
438---     as in [e custom assn at level 99] in the notation below.  Leaving out the
439---     "at level 99" is *semantically equivalent*, because the [assn] grammar starts
440---     at that level, but omitting it will not work because the grammar for
441---     Hoare triples below includes "at level 99" -- the [LEVEL "99"] part of the
442---     grammar counts for factorization.
443---
444---     The upshot is that means that this notation and the Hoare triple notation
445---     (which overlaps with [{{ _ }}]) must be changed in tandem and use identical
446---     level specifications.`

475--- ### Assertion Implication
476-
477--- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
478--- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
479-
480-def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
481-  ∀ st, P st → Q st
482-
483--- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
484--- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
485-
486-notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
487-
488-theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
489-
490--- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
491-
492-notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
493-
494--- Note to developers (Claude):
495---     The Rocq source puts these notations in a `hoare_spec_scope`, with a
496---     book comment explaining that "the `hoare_spec_scope` annotation tells
497---     Rocq that this notation is not global but is intended to be used in
498---     particular contexts." Lean has no notation scopes, so the notations are
499---     simply global and that paragraph is omitted.

501--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
502-
503--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
504--- command. The standard notation is
505-
506---   {P} c {Q}
507-
508--- meaning:
509-
510--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
511--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
512--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
513-
514--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
515--- *postcondition*.
516-
517--- Because single braces are already used for other things in Lean, we'll
518--- write Hoare triples with double braces:
519-
520---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
521-
522--- For example,
523-
524--- - The Hoare triple
525-
526---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
527-
528--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
529--- a state in which `X = 1`.
530-
531--- - On the other hand,
532-
533---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
534-
535--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
536--- `{{X = m}} X :=
537--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
538--- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
539--- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
540-

542-
543--- Paraphrase the following in English.
544-
545---   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
546-
547---   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
548-
549---   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}

551---   4) {{True}} c {{False}}

553---   5) ∀ m,
554---        {{X = m}}
555---        c
556---        {{Y = real_fact m}}
557-
558---   6) ∀ m,
559---        {{X = m}}
560---        c
561---        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}

563--- _Quiz:_
564-
565--- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
566--- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
567-

687--- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
688-
689--- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
690-
691-def ValidHoareTriple
692-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
693-  ∀ st st',
694-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
695-    P st →
696-    Q st'
697-
698--- Note to developers:
699---     `NOTATION: SAZ 2024 One trickiness of these notations is that we
700---     want the [com] and [assn] grammars to be "open", so that they can
701---     include expressions parsed by the full [constr] grammar of Rocq.
702---     However, then there is a conflict of precedence of the
703---     "application" cases:
704---
705---     The example " {{ True }} X := 0 {{ False }} " does not parse as
706---     intended because the [com] grammar includes the capability of
707---     parsing the (ill-typed) term "0 {{ False }}".
708---
709---     This means that the "application" for [com] should disallow
710---     arguments at the level at which the [assn] grammar is included
711---     in constr.  The upshot is that this notation should be included
712---     in the grammar at the *same* level as the assertion notation
713---     [{{ P }}], which is 2.`
714-
715--- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
716--- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
717--- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
718--- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.

728-  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
729-      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))

731-end ValidHoareTriple

784--- ## Proof Rules
785-
786--- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
787--- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
788--- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
789--- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
790--- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
791--- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
792--- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
793--- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
794--- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
795-
796--- ### Skip
797-
798--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
799-
800---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
801---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
802-
803-theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
804-    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
805-  intro st st' h hp
806-  inversion h
807-  assumption
808-
809--- ### Sequencing
810-
811--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
812--- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
813--- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
814--- where `R` holds:
815-
816---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
817---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
818---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
819---   {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
820-
821-theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
822-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
823-    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{ R }} := by
824-  intro st st' h12 pre
825-  inversion h12 with
826-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
827-    exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
828-
829--- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
830--- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
831--- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
832--- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
833--- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
834--- through commands until we reach the beginning.
835-
836--- ### Assignment
837-
838--- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
839--- rules. Here's how it works.
840-
841--- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
842-
843---   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
844-
845--- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
846--- could the precondition be?
847-
848--- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
849--- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
850-
851---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
852-
853--- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
854--- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
855--- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
856--- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
857--- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
858-
859--- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
860-
861---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
862-
863--- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
864--- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
865-
866---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
867-
868--- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
869--- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
870--- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
871--- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
872--- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
873--- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
874--- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
875-
876--- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
877--- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
878--- expression `a`:
879-
880---   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
881-
882--- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
883--- replaced by `a`.
884-
885--- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
886--- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
887-
888--- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
889-
890---   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
891-
892--- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
893--- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
894--- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
895--- for every occurrence of `X`.
896-
897--- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
898--- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
899--- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
900--- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
901-
902--- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
903--- We'll do that later in some exercises.
904-
905--- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
906-
907---   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
908---     X := X + 1
909---   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
910-
911---   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
912---     X := 3
913---   {{ X = 3 }}
914-
915---   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
916---     X := 3
917---   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
918-
919--- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
920--- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
921--- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.sub`.
922-
923--- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
924--- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
925--- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
926-
927--- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
928--- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
929--- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
930--- directly "edit" its text.
931-
932--- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
933--- state, defined as follows:
934-
935-def Assertion.sub (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
936-  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
937-
938--- Note to developers (One An @meluge, before next release):
939---     Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)
940-
941-/-- Assertion substitution: `P [X ↦ a]` -/
942-syntax:100 term:100 " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
943-
944-macro_rules
945-  | `($P [$x ↦ $a]) => `(Assertion.sub $x (aexp { $a }) $P)
946-  -- | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a])) => ``(assn($st; $P) [$x ↦ $a]) -- maybe we could push substitutions inside
947-
948--- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
949-
950---   P [ X ↦ a ]
951-
952-#check (fun st => Assertion.sub X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
953-#check {{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]
954-#check (∀ st, ({{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]) st)
955-
956--- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
957--- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
958--- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
959-
960--- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
961--- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
962--- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
963-
964---   fun st =>
965---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
966---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
967-
968--- which simplifies to
969-
970---   fun st =>
971---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
972---     (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
973-
974--- and further simplifies to
975-
976---   fun st =>
977---     ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
978-
979--- and finally to
980-
981---   fun st =>
982---     3 ≤ 5.
983-
984--- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
985--- expected).
986-
987--- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
988--- X + 1]`.
989--- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
990-
991---   fun st =>
992---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
993---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
994-
995--- which simplifies to
996-
997---   fun st =>
998---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
999-
1000--- and further simplifies to
1001-
1002---   fun st =>
1003---     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1004-
1005--- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.
1006-
1007--- We can demonstrate formally that we have captured intuitive meaning of
1008--- "assertion subsitution" by proving some example logical equivalences:
1009-
1010-namespace ExampleAssertionSub
1011-example :
1012-    {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ 3] <<->> {{ 3 ≤ 5 }} := by
1013-  constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
1014-
1015-example :
1016-    {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ X + 1] <<->> {{ (X + 1) ≤ 5 }} := by
1017-  constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
1018-
1019-end ExampleAssertionSub
1020-
1021--- ### Printing Assertions
1022-
1023--- As in the Imp chapter, the assertion notations above are *input* only: Lean
1024--- reads `{{ X ≤ 5 }}` but still prints the underlying function. The
1025--- delaborators below close the loop for the common cases: Hoare triples,
1026--- `->>` implications, and assertion substitutions are printed back in their
1027--- concrete notation, and an assertion Lean cannot rebuild falls back to the
1028--- raw `fun st => …` form -- which is exactly this notation's escape syntax,
1029--- so what you see is always valid input. As before, there is no need to
1030--- understand the details, and everything can be switched off with
1031--- `set_option pp.notation false`.
1032-
1033--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing assertions back
1034-
1035-namespace Assertion.Delab
1036-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
1037-
1038-/-- Rebuild the surface form of an assertion body, undoing the state
1039-threading the `assn` elaborator performs: `st[X]` prints as `X`,
1040-`Aexp.eval st a` as `a`, `Bexp.eval st b = true` as `b`, an applied
1041-assertion `P st` as `P`, and a subterm that does not mention the state
1042-prints as itself. -/
1043-partial def delabBody (stId : FVarId) : DelabM Term := do
1044-  let e ← getExpr
1045-  if !e.containsFVar stId then
1046-    delab
1047-  else
1048-    match_expr e with
1049-    | MyGetElem.getElem _ _ _ _ st _ =>
1050-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
1051-      withNaryArg 5 delab
1052-    | Aexp.eval st _ =>
1053-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
1054-      withAppArg delab
1055-    | HAdd.hAdd _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
1056-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) + $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
1057-    | HSub.hSub _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
1058-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) - $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
1059-    | HMul.hMul _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
1060-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) * $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
1061-    | Eq _ l r =>
1062-      -- `Bexp.eval st b = true` is the threaded form of a bare boolean `b`
1063-      if r.isConstOf ``Bool.true && l.isAppOfArity ``Bexp.eval 2
1064-          && l.appFn!.appArg! == .fvar stId then
1065-        withNaryArg 1 <| withAppArg delab
1066-      else
1067-        `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) = $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
1068-    | Ne _ _ _ =>
1069-      `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) ≠ $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
1070-    | LE.le _ _ _ _ =>
1071-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≤ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
1072-    | LT.lt _ _ _ _ =>
1073-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) < $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
1074-    | GE.ge _ _ _ _ =>
1075-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≥ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
1076-    | GT.gt _ _ _ _ =>
1077-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) > $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
1078-    | And _ _ =>
1079-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ∧ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
1080-    | Or _ _ =>
1081-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ∨ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
1082-    | Iff _ _ =>
1083-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ↔ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
1084-    | Not _ =>
1085-      `(¬ $(← withAppArg (delabBody stId)))
1086-    | _ =>
1087-      if e.isArrow then
1088-        `($(← withBindingDomain (delabBody stId)) →
1089-          $(← withBindingBody `h (delabBody stId)))
1090-      else if let .app f v := e then
1091-        -- an applied assertion `P st` (or an applied escape lambda)
1092-        guard (v == .fvar stId)
1093-        guard !(f.containsFVar stId)
1094-        withAppFn delab
1095-      else
1096-        failure
1097-
1098-/-- Print an `Assertion`-valued term as it appears inside `{{ … }}`: a
1099-state lambda is un-threaded; a term the printer cannot rebuild falls back
1100-to the raw lambda, which is exactly this notation's escape form. -/
1101-partial def delabAssn : DelabM Term := do
1102-  if (← getExpr).isLambda then
1103-    (withBindingBody' `st (pure ·.fvarId!) fun stId => delabBody stId)
1104-      <|> Delaborator.delab
1105-  else
1106-    delab
1107-
1108-@[delab app.ValidHoareTriple]
1109-def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1110-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``ValidHoareTriple 3
1111-  let P ← withNaryArg 0 delabAssn
1112-  let c ← withNaryArg 1 delabComInner
1113-  let Q ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
1114-  `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
1115-
1116-/-- Print an assertion-position argument: a state lambda gets the
1117-`{{ … }}` notation; any other term (a named assertion, a substitution)
1118-already reads well bare. -/
1119-def delabAssnArg (i : Nat) : DelabM Term := do
1120-  if (← withNaryArg i getExpr).isLambda then
1121-    `({{ $(← withNaryArg i delabAssn) }})
1122-  else
1123-    withNaryArg i Delaborator.delab
1124-
1125-@[delab app.AssertImplies]
1126-def delabAssertImplies : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1127-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
1128-  `($(← delabAssnArg 0) ->> $(← delabAssnArg 1))
1129-
1130-@[delab app.Assertion.sub]
1131-def delabSub : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1132-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``Assertion.sub 3
1133-  let `($x:ident) ← withNaryArg 0 delab | failure
1134-  let a ← withNaryArg 1 delabAexpInner
1135-  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
1136-  if (← withNaryArg 2 getExpr).isLambda then
1137-    `({{ $P }} [$x:ident ↦ $a:imp_aexp])
1138-  else
1139-    `($P [$x:ident ↦ $a:imp_aexp])
1140-
1141-end Assertion.Delab

1144-
1145--- Now, using the substitution operation we've just defined, we can give the
1146--- precise proof rule for assignment:
1147-
1148---   ---------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1149---   {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X := a {{Q}}
1150-
1151--- We can prove formally that this rule is indeed valid.
1152-
1153-theorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
1154-    {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}  x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by
1155-  intro st st' hE hQ
1156-  inversion hE with
1157-  | asgn n h =>
1158-    subst h
1159-    exact hQ

1207--- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_wrong ⭐⭐
1208-
1209--- The assignment rule looks backward to almost everyone the first time they
1210--- see it. If it still seems puzzling to you, it may help to think a little
1211--- about alternative "forward" rules. Here is a seemingly natural one:
1212-
1213---   ------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_wrong)
1214---   {{ True }} X := a {{ X = a }}
1215-
1216--- Give a counterexample showing that this rule is incorrect and use it to
1217--- complete the proof below, showing that it is really a counterexample.
1218--- (Hint: The rule universally quantifies over the arithmetic expression `a`,
1219--- so your counterexample needs to exhibit an `a` for which the rule doesn't
1220--- work.)
1221-
1222-theorem hoare_asgn_wrong : ∃ a : Aexp,
1223-    ¬ {{ True }} X := ~a; {{ X = a }} := by
1224-  all_goals
1225-    exists aexp { X + 1 }
1226-    intro hc
1227-    unfold ValidHoareTriple at hc
1228-    have h2 : (X →ₜ 1 ; ∅)[X] = (aexp { X + 1 }).eval (X →ₜ 1 ; ∅) := by
1229-      apply hc ∅ (X →ₜ 1 ; ∅)
1230-      · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1231-      · exact True.intro
1232-    simp [TotalMap.update_eq] at h2
1233-
1234--- If `a` itself mentions `X`, then the value of `a` may be different in the
1235--- final state because of this update. For example, if `a` is `X + 1`, then
1236--- setting `X` to `a` certainly does not achieve the postcondition
1237--- `X = X + 1`! The underlying problem is that the state in which the
1238--- postcondition will be checked is different than the state in which `a` was
1239--- evaluated when it was assigned to `X`.
1240-
1241--- ### Exercise (3 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1242-
1243--- By using a *parameter* `m` (a Lean number) to remember the original value
1244--- of `X` we can define a Hoare rule for assignment that does, intuitively,
1245--- "work forwards" rather than backwards.
1246-
1247---   ------------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd)
1248---   {{fun st => P st ∧ st[X] = m}}
1249---     X := a
1250---   {{fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧ st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1251-
1252--- Note that we need to write out the postcondition in "desugared" form,
1253--- because it needs to talk about two different states: we use the original
1254--- value of `X` to reconstruct the state `st'` before the assignment took
1255--- place. (Also note that this rule is more complicated than `hoare_asgn`!)
1256-
1257--- Prove that this rule is correct.
1258-
1259--- Note to developers:
1260---     HIDE: BCP 21: Could we make the precondition use compact notation, at
1261---     least?
1262---
1263---     HIDE: SAZ 2024 - this version of the syntax does let us use the compact
1264---     notation for the precondition, but it comes at the cost of having to
1265---     "escape" the function in the postcondition.
1266-
1267-theorem hoare_asgn_fwd (m : Nat) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) :
1268-    {{ P ∧ X = m }}
1269-      X := ~a;
1270-    {{ fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st)
1271-         ∧ st[X] = a.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) }} := by
1272-  all_goals
1273-    unfold ValidHoareTriple
1274-    intro st st' heval hpre
1275-    inversion heval with
1276-    | asgn n h =>
1277-      obtain ⟨hp, hx⟩ := hpre
1278-      subst h
1279-      have hx' : st[X] = m := hx
1280-      rw [← hx', TotalMap.update_eq, TotalMap.update_shadow,
1281-          TotalMap.update_same]
1282-      exact ⟨hp, rfl⟩
1283-
1284--- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd_exists (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1285-
1286--- Another way to define a forward rule for assignment is to existentially
1287--- quantify over the previous value of the assigned variable. Prove that it is
1288--- correct.
1289-
1290---   ------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd_exists)
1291---   {{fun st => P st}}
1292---     X := a
1293---   {{fun st => ∃ m, P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧
1294---                  st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1295-
1296-theorem hoare_asgn_fwd_exists (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) :
1297-    {{ P }}
1298-      X := ~a;
1299-    {{ fun st => ∃ m, P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧
1300-         st[X] = a.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) }} := by
1301-  all_goals
1302-    unfold ValidHoareTriple
1303-    intro st st' heval hpre
1304-    inversion heval with
1305-    | asgn n h =>
1306-      subst h
1307-      exists st[X]
1308-      rw [TotalMap.update_eq, TotalMap.update_shadow, TotalMap.update_same]
1309-      exact ⟨hpre, rfl⟩

1311--- ### Consequence
1312-
1313--- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare rules
1314--- won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at hand -- they
1315--- may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails
1316--- to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually may be
1317--- logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
1318--- what we need.
1319-
1320--- For instance,
1321-
1322---   {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1323-
1324--- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1325-
1326---   {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1327-
1328--- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of `hoare_asgn`
1329--- because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal
1330--- assertions.
1331-
1332--- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid, then
1333--- the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this observation with
1334--- the following rule:
1335-
1336---      {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1337---        P <<->> P'
1338---   ---------------------
1339---      {{P}} c {{Q}}
1340-
1341--- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that strengthening
1342--- the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a valid triple always
1343--- produces another valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules
1344--- of Consequence*.
1345-
1346---          {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1347---             P ->> P'
1348---   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1349---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1350-
1351---          {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1352---            Q' ->> Q
1353---   -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1354---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1355-
1356--- Here are the formal versions:
1357-
1358-theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1359-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1360-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1361-  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1362-  intro st st' heval hpre
1363-  apply hhoare st st'
1364-  · assumption
1365-  · apply himp
1366-    assumption
1367-
1368-theorem hoare_consequence_post (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1369-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1370-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1371-  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1372-  intro st st' heval hpre
1373-  apply himp
1374-  apply hhoare st st'
1375-  · assumption
1376-  · assumption
1377-
1378--- For example, we can use the first consequence rule like this:
1379-
1380---   {{ True }} ->>
1381---   {{ (X = 1) [X ↦ 1] }}
1382---     X := 1
1383---   {{ X = 1 }}
1384-
1385--- Or, formally...
1386-
1387-theorem hoare_asgn_example1 :
1388-    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1389-  all_goals
1390-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1391-    · apply hoare_asgn
1392-    · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1393-      intro st _
1394-      rfl
1395-
1396--- We can also use it to prove the example mentioned earlier.
1397-
1398---   {{ X < 4 }} ->>
1399---   {{ (X < 5)[X ↦ X + 1] }}
1400---     X := X + 1
1401---   {{ X < 5 }}
1402-
1403--- Or, formally ...
1404-
1405-theorem assertion_sub_example2 :
1406-    {{X < 4}}
1407-      X := X + 1;
1408-    {{X < 5}} := by
1409-  all_goals
1410-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1411-    · apply hoare_asgn
1412-    · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1413-      intro st h
1414-      simp [TotalMap.update_eq] at *
1415-      lia
1416-
1417--- Finally, here is a combined rule of consequence that allows us to vary both
1418--- the precondition and the postcondition.
1419-
1420---          {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1421---             P ->> P'
1422---             Q' ->> Q
1423---   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
1424---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1425-
1426-theorem hoare_consequence (P P' Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1427-    (htriple : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :
1428-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1429-  apply hoare_consequence_pre (P' := P')
1430-  · apply hoare_consequence_post (Q' := Q')
1431-    · assumption
1432-    · assumption
1433-  · assumption
1434-
1435--- ### Automation
1436-
1437--- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples can be
1438--- streamlined using the automation techniques that we introduced in the
1439--- *Automation* chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1440-
1441--- Recall that the `simp` tactic can be told to unfold definitions as part of
1442--- its simplifications. The definitions we keep needing to unfold in this
1443--- chapter are `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, `Assertion.sub`, the
1444--- lifting functions `Assertion.ofProp`, `Aexp'.ofNat`, and `Aexp'.ofAexp`,
1445--- and the total-map operations. We'll pass these to `simp` explicitly below
1446--- (and shortly package the recipe up as a tactic of our own).
1447-
1448--- Note to developers (Claude):
1449---     The Rocq source here registers
1450---     `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1451---     t_update : core` for `auto`.
1452---     That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the `Arguments /.` commands,
1453---     it does not affect `simpl`), so its Lean counterpart is the
1454---     `assertion_auto` tactic's simp list below -- not global `@[simp]`
1455---     lemmas as for the notation wrappers, whose folded names carry no
1456---     meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.sub` do.
1457-
1458--- The proof of `hoare_consequence_pre`, repeated below, looks like an
1459--- opportune place for automation, because all it does is `unfold`, `intro`,
1460--- and `apply`. (It uses `assumption`, too, but that's just application of a
1461--- hypothesis.)
1462-
1463-theorem hoare_consequence_pre' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1464-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1465-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1466-  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1467-  intro st st' heval hpre
1468-  apply hhoare st st'
1469-  · assumption
1470-  · apply himp
1471-    assumption
1472-
1473--- Notice that this proof passes the states `st` and `st'` to `apply
1474--- hhoare`
1475--- explicitly. We didn't actually need to: when an argument of the applied
1476--- theorem is not determined by the goal, `apply` introduces a *metavariable*
1477--- `?st` as a placeholder and lets a later step of the proof determine it.
1478--- Here, `assumption` instantiates `?st` with `st` when it discovers `st` in
1479--- the assumption `heval`. Using `apply` this way is like telling Lean, "Be
1480--- patient: The missing part is going to be filled in later in the proof."
1481-
1482-theorem hoare_consequence_pre''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1483-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1484-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1485-  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1486-  intro st st' heval hpre
1487-  apply hhoare
1488-  · assumption
1489-  · apply himp
1490-    assumption
1491-
1492--- Since the remaining steps just apply hypotheses to each other, the entire
1493--- proof can actually be compressed into a single line, by writing the term
1494--- that `exact`ly proves the conclusion.
1495-
1496-theorem hoare_consequence_pre'''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1497-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1498-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1499-  intro st st' heval hpre
1500-  exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
1501-
1502--- Of course, it's hard to write such a one-liner without having gone through
1503--- the original proof of `hoare_consequence_pre` to see the steps it used. But
1504--- now that we know the shape of the argument, it's a good bet that the same
1505--- trick will also work for `hoare_consequence_post`.
1506-
1507-theorem hoare_consequence_post' (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1508-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1509-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1510-  intro st st' heval hpre
1511-  exact himp st' (hhoare st st' heval hpre)
1512-
1513--- We can also use a metavariable to streamline a proof
1514--- (`hoare_asgn_example1`), that we did earlier as an example of using the
1515--- consequence rule:
1516-
1517-theorem hoare_asgn_example1' :
1518-    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1519-  apply hoare_consequence_pre  -- no need to state an assertion
1520-  · apply hoare_asgn
1521-  · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1522-    intro st _
1523-    rfl
1524-
1525--- The final bullet of that proof also looks like a candidate for automation.
1526-
1527-theorem hoare_asgn_example1'' :
1528-    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1529-  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1530-  · apply hoare_asgn
1531-  · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, TotalMap.update_eq]
1532-
1533--- Now we have quite a nice proof script: it simply identifies the Hoare rules
1534--- that need to be used and leaves the remaining low-level details up to Lean
1535--- to figure out.
1536-
1537--- By now it might be apparent that the *entire* proof could be automated by a
1538--- more ambitious tactic that also knew about the Hoare rules themselves. We
1539--- won't build one in this chapter, so that we can get a better understanding
1540--- of when and how the Hoare rules are used. In the next chapter, *Hoare2*,
1541--- we'll dive deeper into automating entire proofs of Hoare triples.
1542-
1543--- The other example of using consequence that we did earlier,
1544--- `hoare_asgn_example2`, requires a little more work to automate. `simp`
1545--- simplifies the assertion implication in the final bullet, but cannot finish
1546--- it: the leftover goal is arithmetic, so it needs `lia`.
1547-
1548-theorem assertion_sub_example2' :
1549-    {{X < 4}}
1550-      X := X + 1;
1551-    {{X < 5}} := by
1552-  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1553-  · apply hoare_asgn
1554-  · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, TotalMap.update_eq]  -- an arithmetic goal remains
1555-    lia
1556-
1557--- Let's introduce our own tactic to handle both that bullet and the bullet
1558--- from example 1. A `macro` declaration gives a name to a canned sequence of
1559--- tactics:
1560-
1561-/-- Prove routine facts about assertions: unfold the Hoare-logic
1562-definitions and lifting functions, simplify, and finish any leftover
1563-arithmetic with `lia`. -/
1564-macro "assertion_auto" : tactic =>
1565-  `(tactic| (intros
1566-             <;> try (simp [assertImplies_def, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
1567-                            W, X, Y, Z] at *)
1568-             <;> try lia))
1569-
1570-theorem assertion_sub_example2'' :
1571-    {{X < 4}}
1572-      X := X + 1;
1573-    {{X < 5}} := by
1574-  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1575-  · apply hoare_asgn
1576-  · assertion_auto
1577-
1578-theorem hoare_asgn_example1''' :
1579-    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1580-  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1581-  · apply hoare_asgn
1582-  · assertion_auto
1583-
1584--- Again, we have quite a nice proof script. All the low-level details of
1585--- proofs about assertions have been taken care of automatically. Of course,
1586--- `assertion_auto` isn't able to prove everything we could possibly want to
1587--- know about assertions -- there's no magic here! But it's pretty good.

1612--- ### Sequencing + Assignment
1613-
1614--- Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and assignment.
1615--- Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with `hoare_consequence_pre` and
1616--- `apply`'s metavariables.
1617-
1618-theorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1619-    {{a = n}}
1620-      X := ~a;
1621-      skip;
1622-    {{X = n}} := by
1623-  apply hoare_seq
1624-  · -- right part of seq
1625-    apply hoare_skip
1626-  · -- left part of seq
1627-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1628-    · apply hoare_asgn
1629-    · assertion_auto
1630-
1631--- Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the sequencing rule is
1632--- as a "decorated program" where the intermediate assertion `Q` is written
1633--- between `c1` and `c2`:
1634-
1635---            {{ a = n }}
1636---   X := a
1637---            {{ X = n }};    <--- decoration for Q
1638---   skip
1639---            {{ X = n }}
1640-
1641--- We'll come back to the idea of decorated programs in much more detail in
1642--- the next chapter.
1643-
1644--- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_example4 ⭐⭐
1645-
1646--- Translate this "decorated program" into a formal proof:
1647-
1648---                  {{ True }} ->>
1649---                  {{ 1 = 1 }}
1650---   X := 1
1651---                  {{ X = 1 }} ->>
1652---                  {{ X = 1 ∧ 2 = 2 }};
1653---   Y := 2
1654---                  {{ X = 1 ∧ Y = 2 }}
1655-
1656--- Note the use of "`->>`" decorations, each marking a use of
1657--- `hoare_consequence_pre`.
1658-
1659--- We've started you off by providing a use of `hoare_seq` that explicitly
1660--- identifies `X = 1` as the intermediate assertion.
1661-
1662-theorem hoare_asgn_example4 :
1663-    {{ True }}
1664-      X := 1;
1665-      Y := 2;
1666-    {{ X = 1 ∧ Y = 2 }} := by
1667-  apply hoare_seq (Q := {{ X = 1 }})
1668-  · -- right part of seq
1669-    all_goals
1670-      apply hoare_consequence_pre
1671-      · apply hoare_asgn
1672-      · assertion_auto
1673-  · -- left part of seq
1674-    all_goals
1675-      apply hoare_consequence_pre
1676-      · apply hoare_asgn
1677-      · assertion_auto

1679--- ### Exercise (3 stars): swap_exercise ⭐⭐⭐
1680-
1681--- Write an Imp program `c` that swaps the values of `X` and `Y` and show that
1682--- it satisfies the following specification:
1683-
1684---   {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
1685-
1686--- Your proof should not need to use `unfold ValidHoareTriple`.
1687-
1688--- Hints:
1689-
1690--- - Remember that Imp commands need to be enclosed in `imp { … }` brackets.
1691-
1692--- - Remember that the assignment rule works best when it's applied "back to
1693---   front," from the postcondition to the precondition. So your proof will want
1694---   to start at the end and work back to the beginning of your program.
1695-
1696--- - Remember that `apply` is your friend.)
1697-
1698--- Note to developers:
1699---     `HIDE: CH: Here goes:
1700---     [[
1701---       {{ X ≤ Y }}

1712---        section, since it's a good warm-up exercise.`

1715-  (imp { Z := X; X := Y; Y := Z; })

1718-    {{X ≤ Y}}
1719-      ~swap_program
1720-    {{Y ≤ X}} := by

1723-    apply hoare_seq

1731--- ### Exercise (4 stars): invalid_triple (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1732-
1733--- Show that
1734-
1735---   {{ a = n }} X := 3; Y := a {{ Y = n }}
1736-
1737--- is not a valid Hoare triple for some choices of `a` and `n`.
1738-
1739--- Conceptual hint: Invent a particular `a` and `n` for which the triple in
1740--- invalid, then use those to complete the proof.
1741-
1742--- Technical hint: Hypothesis `h` below begins `∀ a n, ...`. You'll want to
1743--- instantiate that with the particular `a` and `n` you've invented. You can
1744--- do that with `have` and `apply`, but you may remember (from the
1745--- *Automation* chapter of Logical Foundations) that Lean offers an even
1746--- easier tactic: `specialize`. If you write
1747-
1748---   specialize h your_a your_n
1749-
1750--- the hypothesis will be instantiated on `your_a` and `your_n`.
1751-
1752--- Having chosen your `a` and `n`, proceed as follows:
1753-
1754--- - Use the (assumed) validity of the given hoare triple to derive a state
1755---   `st'` in which `Y` has some value `y1`
1756-
1757--- - Use the evaluation rules (`Com.EvalR.seq` and `Com.EvalR.asgn`) to show
1758---   that `Y` has a *different* value `y2` in the same final state `st'`
1759-
1760--- - Since `y1` and `y2` are both equal to `st'[Y]`, they are equal to each
1761---   other. But we chose them to be different, so this is a contradiction, which
1762---   finishes the proof.
1763-
1764-theorem invalid_triple : ¬ ∀ (a : Aexp) (n : Nat),
1765-    {{ a = n }}
1766-      X := 3; Y := ~a;
1767-    {{ Y = n }} := by
1768-  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1769-  intro h
1770-  all_goals
1771-    specialize h (aexp { X }) 2 (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) (Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅)
1772-    have heval : (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) =[ X := 3; Y := X; ]=>
1773-        (Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
1774-      apply Com.EvalR.seq
1775-      · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1776-      · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1777-    apply h at heval
1778-    have hcontra := heval rfl
1779-    simp [TotalMap.update_eq] at hcontra

1781--- ### Conditionals
1782-
1783--- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1784-
1785--- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of the
1786--- branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be tempted
1787--- to write:
1788-
1789---           {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1790---           {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1791---   ---------------------------------
1792---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1793-
1794--- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot show
1795-
1796---   {{ True }}
1797---     if X = 0
1798---       then Y := 2
1799---       else Y := X + 1
1800---     end
1801---   {{ X ≤ Y }}
1802-
1803--- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1804--- assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1805-
1806--- Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch, we
1807--- know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the "else"
1808--- branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information available
1809--- in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work with when
1810--- reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the reasons why they
1811--- establish the postcondition `Q`).
1812-
1813---   {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1814---   {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1815---   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1816---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1817-
1818--- Strictly speaking, `P ∧ b` combines an assertion with a boolean expression.
1819--- The assertion notation handles this by evaluating `b` in the current state.
1820--- We'll write `bassertion b` for the resulting assertion: "the boolean
1821--- expression `b` evaluates to `true` in the given state."
1822-
1823-def bassertion (b : Bexp) : Assertion := {{ b }}
1824-
1825-@[simp] theorem bassertion_apply (b : Bexp) (st : State) :
1826-    bassertion b st = (b.eval st = true) := rfl
1827-
1828-instance : Coe Bexp Assertion := ⟨bassertion⟩
1829-
1830--- A useful fact about `bassertion`:
1831-
1832--- Note to developers (before next release):
1833---     `Robert Rand: This isn't an identity but that's because
1834---     we're using [~(bassertion b st)] in our triples, instead of a more
1835---     direct/intuitive predicate.
1836---
1837---     Some alternatives: 1) P_True b and P_False b (defined directly as
1838---     desired) 1) bassertion b false (adds relevant argument to bassertion)
1839---     2) ((bassertion (!b)) st) (clearer, but less direct).`
1840-
1841-theorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
1842-    ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1843-  simp [h]
1844-
1845--- Here `simp` is able to find that `b.eval st` is assumed to be `false` (by
1846--- rewriting with `h`), notice that the goal claims it is `true`, and use the
1847--- resulting contradiction to complete the proof.
1848-
1849--- Note to developers (One An @meluge):
1850---     The Rocq proof is the single tactic `congruence`. Using simp seems to
1851---     work but should we build our own `congruence` tactic?
1852-
1853--- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals and prove it
1854--- correct.
1855-
1856--- The statement of the rule reads: given `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1857--- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1858--- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1859-
1860--- That is (unwrapping the notations):
1861-
1862---   theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
1863---       (htrue : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ bassertion b st) c1 Q)
1864---       (hfalse : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ ¬ (bassertion b st)) c2 Q) :
1865---       ValidHoareTriple P (Com.cond b c1 c2) Q
1866-
1867-theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
1868-    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1869-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1870-  intro st st' hE hP
1871-  inversion hE with
1872-  | ifTrue hb hc => exact htrue _ _ hc ⟨hP, hb⟩
1873-  | ifFalse hb hc => exact hfalse _ _ hc ⟨hP, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
1874-
1875--- #### Example
1876-
1877--- Here is a formal proof that the program we used to motivate the rule
1878--- satisfies the specification we wanted.
1879-
1880-theorem if_example :
1881-    {{True}}
1882-      if (X = 0) {
1883-        Y := 2;
1884-      } else {
1885-        Y := X + 1;
1886-      }
1887-    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1888-  -- the proof is the same for both the true and false branches
1889-  apply hoare_if <;>
1890-  · apply hoare_consequence_pre
1891-    · apply hoare_asgn
1892-    · assertion_auto

1895--- script that isn't about the Hoare rules. Unfortunately, the
1896--- `assertion_auto` tactic we wrote wasn't quite up to the job. Looking at the
1897--- proof of `if_example`, we can see why: we had to unfold a definition
1898--- (`bassertion`) that we didn't need in earlier proofs. (The step from the
1899--- boolean equality test `st[X] == 0` to the equation `st[X] = 0` is handled
1900--- by lemmas `simp` already knows, such as `beq_iff_eq`.) So, let's add the
1901--- unfolding into our tactic.

1957--- #### Exercise: One-sided conditionals
1958-
1959--- Note to developers:
1960---     HIDE: Question from 2012, Midterm 2. One-sided conditionals.
1961-
1962--- In this exercise we consider extending Imp with "one-sided conditionals" of
1963--- the form `if1 (b) { c }`. Here `b` is a boolean expression, and `c` is a
1964--- command. If `b` evaluates to `true`, then command `c` is evaluated. If `b`
1965--- evaluates to `false`, then `if1 (b) { c }` does nothing.
1966-
1967--- We recommend that you complete this exercise before attempting the ones
1968--- that follow, as it should help solidify your understanding of the material.
1969-
1970--- The first step is to extend the syntax of commands and introduce the usual
1971--- notations. (We've done this for you, in a separate namespace to prevent
1972--- polluting the global name space. The `scoped` notations below are active
1973--- only inside `namespace If1`.)
1974-
1975-end -- closes `open scoped ValidHoareTriple`
1976-namespace If1
1977-
1978-inductive Com : Type where
1979-  | skip : Com
1980-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
1981-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
1982-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
1983-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
1984-  | if1 : Bexp → Com → Com
1985-
1986-/-- If1 commands: Imp commands plus `if1` -/
1987-declare_syntax_cat if1_com
1988-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
1989-syntax ident ";" : if1_com
1990-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
1991-syntax if1_com ppDedent(ppLine if1_com) : if1_com
1992-/-- Assignment -/
1993-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : if1_com
1994-/-- Conditional -/
1995-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
1996-/-- Loop -/
1997-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
1998-/-- One-sided conditional -/
1999-syntax "if1 " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2000-/-- Escape to Lean -/
2001-syntax:max "~" term:max : if1_com
2002-
2003-/-- Include an If1 command in Lean code -/
2004-syntax:min "imp1" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2005-
2006-open Lean in

2008-  | `(imp1 { $x:ident ; }) =>
2009-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2010-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2011-  | `(imp1 { $c1 $c2 }) =>
2012-    `(Com.seq (imp1 {$c1}) (imp1 {$c2}))
2013-  | `(imp1 { $x:ident := $a; }) =>

2015-  | `(imp1 { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>

2021-  | `(imp1 { ~$c }) =>

2038-      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :

2040-  | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
2041-      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :

2046-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2047-      (hloop : EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :

2185--- ### While Loops
2186-
2187--- The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a *command
2188--- invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion whose truth is guaranteed
2189--- after executing a command, assuming it is true before.
2190-
2191--- That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
2192-
2193---   {{P}} c {{P}}
2194-
2195--- holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily become false in
2196--- the middle of executing `c`, but by the end of `c` it must be restored.
2197-
2198--- As a first attempt at a `while` rule, we could try:
2199-
2200---          {{P}} c {{P}}
2201---   ---------------------------
2202---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P}}
2203-
2204--- This rule is valid: if `P` is a command invariant of `c`, as the premise
2205--- requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body executes, `P` is
2206--- going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
2207-
2208--- But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the loop
2209--- terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the postcondition
2210--- in the conclusion:
2211-
2212---           {{P}} c {{P}}
2213---   ---------------------------------
2214---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2215-
2216--- Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can also
2217--- strengthen the precondition in the premise:
2218-
2219---         {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2220---   --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
2221---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2222-
2223--- That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip` and
2224--- conditionals:
2225-
2226--- - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that the
2227---   precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
2228-
2229--- - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
2230---   subcommand.
2231-
2232--- Note to developers:
2233---     HIDE: The big comment will not display nicely. But I guess it's
2234---     folded...
2235-
2236-theorem hoare_while (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2237-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
2238-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
2239-  intro st st' heval hP
2240-  /- We proceed by induction on `heval`, because, in the "keep
2241-  looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
2242-  of just `c`. The auxiliary statement `key` generalizes over an

2286--- We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
2287-
2288---   {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2289-
2290--- is a valid Hoare triple.
2291-
2292--- This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body whenever the
2293--- loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`, this holds trivially since the
2294--- precondition is false.
2295-
2296--- For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
2297-
2298---   while X = 2 do X := 1 end
2299-
2300--- since the program will never enter the loop.

2449--- If the loop never terminates, any postcondition will work.

2451-theorem always_loop_hoare (Q : Assertion) :
2452-    {{True}} while (true) { skip; } {{ Q }} := by
2453-  apply hoare_consequence_post
2454-  · apply hoare_while
2455-    apply hoare_post_true
2456-    intro st
2457-    exact True.intro
2458-  · intro st ⟨_hinv, hguard⟩
2459-    exact absurd rfl hguard
2460-
2461--- Of course, this result is not surprising if we remember that the definition
2462--- of `ValidHoareTriple` asserts that the postcondition must hold *only* when
2463--- the command terminates. If the command doesn't terminate, we can prove
2464--- anything we like about the post-condition.
2465-
2466--- Hoare rules that specify what happens *if* commands terminate, without
2467--- proving that they do, are said to describe a logic of *partial*
2468--- correctness. It is also possible to give Hoare rules for *total*
2469--- correctness, which additionally specifies that commands must terminate.
2470--- Total correctness is out of the scope of this textbook.

2485--- In this exercise, we'll add a new command to our language of commands:
2486--- `repeat { c } until (b)`. You will write the evaluation rule for `repeat`
2487--- and add a new Hoare rule to the language for programs involving it.

2492-inductive Com : Type where
2493-  | skip : Com
2494-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2495-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2496-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2497-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2498-  | repeatUntil : Com → Bexp → Com

2500--- `repeat` behaves like `while`, except that the loop guard is checked
2501--- *after* each execution of the body, with the loop repeating as long as the
2502--- guard stays *false*. Because of this, the body will always execute at least
2503--- once.

2505-/-- Repeat-Imp commands: Imp commands plus `repeat` -/
2506-declare_syntax_cat rpt_com
2507-/-- Repeat loop -/
2508-syntax "repeat" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") " until " "(" imp_bexp ")" : rpt_com
2509-
2510-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
2511-syntax ident ";" : rpt_com
2512-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
2513-syntax rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine rpt_com) : rpt_com
2514-/-- Assignment -/
2515-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : rpt_com
2516-/-- Conditional -/
2517-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : rpt_com
2518-/-- Loop -/
2519-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : rpt_com

2521-syntax:max "~" term:max : rpt_com

2551-  | skip (st : State) :

2559-      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :

2561-  | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
2562-      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :

2564-  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :

2566-  | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2567-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2568-      (hloop : EvalR (impr {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :
2569-      EvalR (impr {while (~b) {~c} }) st st''

2574-      (hc : EvalR c st st') (hb : b.eval st' = false)
2575-      (hloop : EvalR (impr {repeat {~c} until (~b) }) st' st'') :

2627-/- Here is a very precise version of `hoare_repeat`. -/
2628-/- LATER: A student in 2013 pointed out that this rule is OK as far
2629-as it goes, but it isn't going to lead to a nice rule for decorated
2630-programs, when we get to that, because it uses c twice, perhaps in
2631-different ways! -/
2632-
2633-theorem hoare_repeat (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2634-    (h1 : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }}) (h2 : {{ Q ∧ ¬ b }} ~c {{ Q }}) :
2635-    {{ P }} repeat { ~c } until (~b) {{ Q ∧ b }} := by
2636-  have key : ∀ (cmd : Com) (s s' : State), (s =[ cmd ]=> s') →
2637-      cmd = (impr { repeat { ~c } until (~b) }) →
2638-      ∀ (P' : Assertion), ({{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) → P' s →
2639-      Q s' ∧ bassertion b s' := by
2640-    intro cmd s s' hev
2641-    induction hev with
2642-    | repeatEnd s0 s0' b0 c0 hc hb =>
2643-        intro heq P' hP'c hp
2644-        injection heq with e1 e2
2645-        subst e1 e2
2646-        exact ⟨hP'c _ _ hc hp, hb⟩
2647-    | repeatLoop s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hc hb hloop ih1 ih2 =>
2648-        intro heq P' hP'c hp
2649-        injection heq with e1 e2
2650-        subst e1 e2
2651-        apply ih2 rfl _ h2
2652-        exact ⟨hP'c _ _ hc hp, bexp_eval_false _ _ hb⟩
2653-    | skip s0 => intro heq; simp at heq
2654-    | asgn s0 a n x h => intro heq; simp at heq
2655-    | seq c1 c2 s0 s0' s0'' hh1 hh2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp at heq
2656-    | ifTrue s0 s0' b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
2657-    | ifFalse s0 s0' b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
2658-    | whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
2659-    | whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
2660-        intro heq; simp at heq
2661-  intro st st' heval hpre
2662-  exact key _ st st' heval rfl P h1 hpre

2695-    {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by

2703-theorem hoare_consequence (P P' Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
2704-    (hht : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hPP' : P ->> P') (hQ'Q : Q' ->> Q) :
2705-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
2706-  intro st st' hc hP
2707-  apply hQ'Q
2708-  apply hht st st'
2709-  · assumption
2710-  · apply hPP'
2711-    assumption
2712-
2713-theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
2714-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
2715-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
2716-  intro st st' hc hP
2717-  apply hhoare st st'
2718-  · assumption
2719-  · apply himp
2720-    assumption

2723-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{R}}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
2724-    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{R}} := by
2725-  intro st st' h12 pre
2726-  inversion h12 with
2727-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>

2857--- ## Summary
2858-
2859--- So far, we've introduced Hoare Logic as a tool for reasoning about Imp
2860--- programs.
2861-
2862--- The rules of Hoare Logic are:
2863-
2864---          --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
2865---          {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
2866-
2867---          --------------------  (hoare_skip)
2868---          {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
2869-
2870---            {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
2871---            {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
2872---           ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
2873---           {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
2874-
2875---           {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
2876---           {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
2877---   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
2878---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
2879-
2880---            {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2881---     -----------------------------------  (hoare_while)
2882---     {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
2883-
2884---             {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
2885---                P ->> P'
2886---                Q' ->> Q
2887---      -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
2888---             {{P}} c {{Q}}
2889-
2890--- Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules of Hoare
2891--- logic, and prove that the definitions are sound. Having done so, we can go
2892--- on and work *within* Hoare logic to prove that particular programs satisfy
2893--- particular Hoare triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how Hoare logic is
2894--- can be used to prove that more interesting programs satisfy interesting
2895--- specifications of their behavior.
2896-
2897--- Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing the definition of
2898--- Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules of Hoare logic as a closed
2899--- world for reasoning about programs.
2900-

2903--- ### Havoc
2904-
2905--- In this exercise, we will derive proof rules for a `havoc` command, which
2906--- is similar to the nondeterministic `any` expression from the the Imp
2907--- chapter.
2908-

2910--- and big-step semantics of Himp commands.
2911-

2917-  | seq : Com → Com → Com

2927-everything except `havoc`. -/

2966-  | skip (st : State) :

2979-  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :

3034-    {{ fun st => havoc_pre x Q st }} havoc x; {{ Q }} := by

3055-    {{ P }} havoc x;
3056-    {{ fun st => ∃ (n : Nat), ({{ P [x ↦ ~(Aexp.num n)] }}) st }} := by

3059-  ·
3060-    all_goals

3070--- ### Assert and Assume
3071-
3072--- Note to developers (Claude):
3073---     The Rocq exercise region extends to End HoareAssertAssume. The
3074---     directive here covers only the initial student tasks because Verso
3075---     cannot compile the whole module as one block.
3076-
3077--- In this exercise, we will extend IMP with two commands, `assert` and
3078--- `assume`. Both commands are ways to indicate that a certain assertion
3079--- should hold any time this part of the program is reached. However they
3080--- differ as follows:
3081-
3082--- - If an `assert` statement fails, it causes the program to go into an error
3083---   state and exit.
3084-
3085--- - If an `assume` statement fails, the program fails to evaluate at all. In
3086---   other words, the program gets stuck and has no final state.
3087-
3088--- The new set of commands is:
3089-
3090-namespace HoareAssertAssume
3091-
3092-inductive Com : Type where
3093-  | skip : Com
3094-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
3095-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
3096-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
3097-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
3098-  | assert : Bexp → Com
3099-  | assume : Bexp → Com
3100-
3101--- Note to developers:
3102---     NOTATION: LATER: Reconsider these precedences
3103-
3104-/-- Imp commands plus `assert` and `assume` -/
3105-declare_syntax_cat haa_com
3106-/-- Assert / assume (`assert (b);`, `assume (b);`).  As with `skip`, the
3107-words `assert` and `assume` are not reserved: the production accepts any
3108-identifier and the macro below rejects everything else. -/
3109-syntax ident " (" imp_bexp ")" ";" : haa_com
3110-
3111-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
3112-syntax ident ";" : haa_com
3113-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
3114-syntax haa_com ppDedent(ppLine haa_com) : haa_com
3115-/-- Assignment -/
3116-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : haa_com
3117-/-- Conditional -/
3118-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : haa_com
3119-/-- Loop -/
3120-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : haa_com
3121-/-- Escape to Lean -/
3122-syntax:max "~" term:max : haa_com
3123-
3124-/-- Include an assert/assume-Imp command in Lean code -/
3125-syntax:min "impa" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
3126-
3127-open Lean in
3128-macro_rules
3129-  | `(impa { $x:ident ; }) =>
3130-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
3131-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
3132-  | `(impa { $h:ident ($b) ; }) =>
3133-    if h.getId == `assert then `(Com.assert (bexp {$b}))
3134-    else if h.getId == `assume then `(Com.assume (bexp {$b}))
3135-    else Macro.throwErrorAt h s!"expected 'assert' or 'assume', got '{h.getId}'"
3136-  | `(impa { $c1 $c2 }) =>
3137-    `(Com.seq (impa {$c1}) (impa {$c2}))
3138-  | `(impa { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
3139-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
3140-  | `(impa { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
3141-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (impa {$c1}) (impa {$c2}))
3142-  | `(impa { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
3143-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (impa {$c}))
3144-  | `(impa { ~$c }) =>

3147--- To define the behavior of `assert` and `assume`, we need to add notation
3148--- for an error, which indicates that an assertion has failed. We modify the
3149--- `Com.EvalR` relation, therefore, so that it relates a start state to either
3150--- an end state or to `error`. The `Result` type indicates the end value of a
3151--- program, either a state or an error:
3152-
3153-inductive Result : Type where
3154-  | normal : State → Result
3155-  | error : Result
3156-
3157--- Now we are ready to give you the evaluation relation for the new language.
3158-
3159-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → Result → Prop where
3160-  /- Old rules, several modified -/
3161-  | skip (st : State) :
3162-      EvalR (impa {skip;}) st (.normal st)
3163-  | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
3164-      EvalR (impa {x := ~a;}) st (.normal (x →ₜ n ; st))
3165-  | seqNormal (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' : State) (r : Result)
3166-      (h1 : EvalR c1 st (.normal st')) (h2 : EvalR c2 st' r) :
3167-      EvalR (impa {~c1 ~c2}) st r
3168-  | seqError (c1 c2 : Com) (st : State) (h : EvalR c1 st .error) :
3169-      EvalR (impa {~c1 ~c2}) st .error
3170-  | ifTrue (st : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
3171-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c1 st r) :
3172-      EvalR (impa {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
3173-  | ifFalse (st : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
3174-      (hb : b.eval st = false) (hc : EvalR c2 st r) :
3175-      EvalR (impa {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
3176-  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3177-      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st (.normal st)
3178-  | whileTrueNormal (st st' : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
3179-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st (.normal st'))
3180-      (hloop : EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st' r) :
3181-      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st r
3182-  | whileTrueError (st : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
3183-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st .error) :
3184-      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st .error
3185-  /- Rules for Assert and Assume -/
3186-  | assertTrue (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3187-      EvalR (impa {assert (~b);}) st (.normal st)
3188-  | assertFalse (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3189-      EvalR (impa {assert (~b);}) st .error
3190-  | assume (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3191-      EvalR (impa {assume (~b);}) st (.normal st)
3192-
3193-scoped notation:40 (priority := high) st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " r:41 =>
3194-  Com.EvalR c st0 r
3195-scoped syntax:40 (priority := high) term:41 " =[ " haa_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
3196-scoped macro_rules
3197-  | `($st0 =[ $c:haa_com ]=> $r) => `($st0 =[ impa { $c } ]=> $r)
3198-
3199--- We redefine hoare triples: Now, `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` means that, whenever
3200--- `c` is started in a state satisfying `P`, and terminates with result `r`,
3201--- then `r` is not an error and the state of `r` satisfies `Q`.
3202-
3203-def ValidHoareTriple
3204-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
3205-  ∀ st r,
3206-    (st =[ c ]=> r) → P st →
3207-    (∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q st')

3210-
3211-/-- Hoare triple over assert/assume-Imp commands -/

3214-macro_rules
3215-  | `({{ $P }} $c:haa_com {{ $Q }}) =>
3216-      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (impa { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))

3218-end ValidHoareTriple

3222--- ### Exercise (4 stars): assert_vs_assume ⭐⭐⭐⭐
3223-
3224--- To test your understanding of this modification, give an example
3225--- precondition and postcondition that are satisfied by the `assume` statement
3226--- but not by the `assert` statement.
3227-
3228-theorem assert_assume_differ : ∃ (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion),
3229-    ({{ P }} assume (~b); {{ Q }})
3230-    ∧ ¬ ({{ P }} assert (~b); {{ Q }}) := by
3231-  all_goals
3232-    exists {{ True }}, bexp { false }, ({{ False }} : Assertion)
3233-    constructor
3234-    · unfold ValidHoareTriple
3235-      intro st r hE _
3236-      inversion hE with
3237-      | assume hb => simp at hb
3238-    · intro hC
3239-      unfold ValidHoareTriple at hC
3240-      have h : ∅ =[ assert (false); ]=> Result.error := by
3241-        apply Com.EvalR.assertFalse
3242-        rfl
3243-      obtain ⟨st', heq, _⟩ := hC ∅ Result.error h True.intro
3244-      simp at heq
